definitions.definition: A risky or daring undertaking or journey.

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, chapter 4, in Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC, part I (The Old Buccaneer), page 30:
quote.text: My heart was beating finely when we two set forth in the cold night upon this dangerous venture.

quote.citation: 1979, Johanna Menzel Meskill, A Chinese Pioneer Family‎[1], Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 191:
quote.text: Other jobs which the governor entrusted to Ch'ao-tung dealt with the economic exploitation of the newly won mountain areas. In the Miao-li region, Ch'ao-tung headed an office for developing the petroleum resources discovered there.³⁸ Without much success during his tenure, the venture was later turned over to private entrepreneurs.

definitions.definition: An event that is not, or cannot be, foreseen.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Kings 22:34:
quote.text: A certain man drew a bow at a venture and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness.

definitions.definition: The thing risked; especially, something sent to sea in trade.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: My ventures are not in one bottom trusted.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To undertake a risky or daring journey.

quote.citation: 1693, Decimus Junius Juvenalis, John Dryden Jun., transl., “[The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis.] The Fourteenth Satyr”, in The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis. Translated into English Verse.  […]  Together with the Satires of Aulus Persius Flaccus. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: who freights a ship to venture on the seas

quote.citation: 1949, Joseph Campbell, “The Hero and the God”, in The Hero with a Thousand Faces:
quote.text: A hero ventures forth from the world of common day into a region of supernatural wonder:  […]

quote.citation: c. 1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life and Death of King Iohn”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: I am afraid; and yet I'll venture it.

Till then they had only exchanged glances of the most casual but now under the brim of her new hat she ventured a look at him and the face that met her gaze there in the twilight, wan and strangely drawn, seemed to her the saddest she had ever seen.

quote.citation: 1939 November, “What the Railways are Doing: Penda's Way—A Station built in a Day”, in Railway Magazine, page 364:
quote.text: [...] Mrs. Bray [...] expressed amazement at the speed with which the station was completed, and ventured the opinion that private contractors could still learn something from the railway companies.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, with at or on) To dare to engage in; to attempt without any certainty of success.
(transitive) To put or send on a venture or chance.
(transitive) To confide in; to rely on; to trust.

quote.citation: 1711, Joseph Addison, “No. 21, Saturday, March 24, 1710-11”, in The Spectator‎[2]:
quote.text: A man would be well enough pleased to buy silks of one whom he would not venture to feel his pulse.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To say something; to offer an opinion.

quote.citation: 2000 January 28, Oliver Burkeman, quoting Heston Blumenthal, “Things that make you go yum”, in The Guardian‎[3], →ISSN:
quote.text: “Unctuous is probably quite a good description, but there's a sweetness, too, and a mouthfeel,” ventures Heston Blumenthal, chef at the Fat Duck at Bray.
